title: John 13:1–17
context: Before the feast, Jesus knows His hour has come to depart to the Father. Having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the end. During supper, knowing the Father had given all things into His hands, He washes the disciples’ feet, including the coming betrayer. Peter resists, then overcorrects. Unless He washes them, they have no share with Him. He interprets the act: a servant is not greater than his lord; they will be blessed if they do these things.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What older interpreters in each camp said about love to the end and the Lord who washes feet.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Having loved his own, he loved them to the end. If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me. I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you. If ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on John 13:1, 8, 15, 17)

reformed.quote: He loved them to the end: his love is constant and invincible. Unless I wash you, you have no part with me: we must be cleansed by him or we are no part of his. He sets before them an example of humility.

verses.text: Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.
verses.arminianNotes:
He knew the hour; He loved His own who were in the world to the end—to the uttermost, through the end. Wesley lingered on that constancy.

His own are loved all the way. The world is where they still are; the love does not wait for them to get out first.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: love constant and invincible, to the end. Hour known, departure to the Father, His own loved.

This verse hangs over Judas’s plot and Peter’s fall. The end will test the love; the love will outlast the test.

verses.text: During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him,
verses.arminianNotes:
The basin will be set down in a room where betrayal is already conceived.

Influence is true and Judas’s heart is active. He is not a puppet only; the putting-in meets a willing interior (v. 27 will show a further entering).
verses.reformedNotes:
Already: the plot is in motion before the towel. Devil and heart are both named.

Jesus washes feet in a room Satan has already visited. Love to the end includes a traitor at table.

verses.text: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and was going to God,
verses.arminianNotes:
The stoop is not identity-loss; it is identity-in-action.

The One with all things in hand picks up a towel. Greatness expresses itself as service they can imitate (v. 15).
verses.reformedNotes:
Given all things / come from / going back: full consciousness of deity’s errand.

Omnipotence stoops to serve. The hands that hold all things wash dirty ones.

verses.text: arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist.
verses.arminianNotes:
Rose, laid aside, took, tied. The verbs are incarnation in miniature.

Watch the Lord undress for work we thought beneath rabbis. The example will be this sequence, not a lecture only.
verses.reformedNotes:
Laid aside outer garments: the visual of 1:14 in a room.

Before the cross’s laying-down, a towel. He interprets His death with a basin.

verses.text: Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Poured, began to wash, wipe. Feet of the Twelve, betrayer included unless John later excepts—and he does not.

He washes people who will fail Him. Grace serves before it is repaid, and often after it will not be.
verses.reformedNotes:
Began to wash: the Lord on the floor.

This is the God of v. 3. The basin is theology.

verses.text: Then he came to Simon Peter. He said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Peter names the scandal: Lord, my feet. The question is reverence misfired.

We still try to protect Jesus from His own gospel. The protest sounds humble and refuses the gift.
verses.reformedNotes:
Do you wash my feet?: correct title, wrong refusal.

The one about to be told he has no share is the one policing the Lord’s hands.

verses.text: Jesus answered him, “You don’t know what I am doing now, but you will understand later.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus contrasts “now” with “afterward.” The cross will interpret the bowl.

They may receive what they do not yet understand. Afterward is resurrection-and-Spirit sight.
verses.reformedNotes:
Not now, afterward: He does not wait on their theory.

Union’s rites often precede comprehension. Peter must submit in the dark.

verses.text: Peter said to him, “You will never wash my feet!” Jesus answered him, “If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Peter’s “never” meets Jesus’ warning of “no part with me.” Wesley: if I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me. Cleansing by Jesus is not optional courtesy.

Classical Arminians: share-with-me is the whole salvation-bond. Refusing His washing is refusing Him; the offer of washing is as serious as the threat of no share.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: we must be cleansed by Him or we are no part of His. Never is Peter’s piety; no share is Jesus’ line.

Washing is Christ’s act. Peter’s never would write him out of the inheritance.
verses.keyContrast: Without Jesus’ washing, no share with Him. Arminians hear an actual warning to a disciple who might refuse the gift. Reformed interpreters usually hear that union depends on Christ’s cleansing, which He will not let Peter’s pride veto.

verses.text: Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Peter swings from “never” to “all over.” Peter still wants to manage the volume of grace.

Zeal without understanding overcorrects. Jesus will scale it back to the wash they need.
verses.reformedNotes:
Hands and head: more water as more love.

Peter’s all-in is still Peter’s program. The Lord will define the bath.

verses.text: Jesus said to him, “Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed, but is completely clean. You are clean, but not all of you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Bathed / feet: once-clean people still need the smaller wash. You are clean, but not every one—Judas already in view.

Justification’s bath and daily feet. Clean is not imaginary; not-every-one is authentic. Remaining dirt on a clean person differs from never having bathed.
verses.reformedNotes:
They are completely clean, except for their feet. You are clean, but not all.

The Eleven’s cleanliness is His verdict (15:3). The exception is the one whose heart the devil already holds.

verses.text: For he knew him who would betray him; therefore he said, “You are not all clean.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He knew. Not all clean is targeted knowledge, not a vague scare.

Knowing does not stop the washing of the betrayer’s feet. Love to the end includes this knowledge.
verses.reformedNotes:
Knew who would betray: the aside interprets v. 10.

The unclean one is not a surprise guest. The sentence was precise.

verses.text: So when he had washed their feet, put his outer garment back on, and sat down again, he said to them, “Do you know what I have done to you?
verses.arminianNotes:
Garments back on, place resumed, then the question. Understanding is now the assignment.

The sign is not self-explanatory enough; He will spell the ethic. We still need both the act and the word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Resumed his place: Lord again, having been servant.

Humiliation comes first, then interpretation. Do you understand is a classroom in a dining room.

verses.text: You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am.
verses.arminianNotes:
Teacher and Lord—they are right. The titles stay; the towel reinterpreted them.

He does not cease to be Lord by washing. Example-ethics still have a Lord.
verses.reformedNotes:
So I am: the titles are true.

Servant-work did not cancel Lordship. It defined it.

verses.text: If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
verses.arminianNotes:
If I, then you ought. The ought is as thick as the titles.

Jesus’ example makes imitation possible. Footwashing as posture toward one another is not optional for people who call Him Lord.
verses.reformedNotes:
Ought: the logic of the greater to the lesser.

The church’s mutual service is deduced from His. No one outranks this basin.

verses.text: For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Example: do as I have done. Wesley: I have given you an example.

Just as is the measure. Creative avoidance of serving one another is already not doing this.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: an example of humility. Just as I have done.

He gave an example, not only an experience. The church is to copy the stoop.

verses.text: Most certainly I tell you, a servant is not greater than his lord, neither is one who is sent greater than he who sent him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Truly, truly: servant < master, messenger < sender. Status-escape is closed.

Sent ones do not outgrow the Sender’s towel. 15:20 will reuse this for persecution.
verses.reformedNotes:
Not greater: two comparisons, one point.

Messengers remain under the sent-Lord. Greatness in this house runs downward.

verses.text: If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Know / if you do: blessing is in the doing. Wesley: happy are ye if ye do them.

Knowledge without doing is not the blessed condition. Grace that teaches also enables the doing it blesses.
verses.reformedNotes:
If you know / if you do: two ifs, blessing on the second.

Understood towels still have to hit feet. Blessing is promised to doers in this school.
